Waiting out a crash in cash: 70 years of treasury bills against inflation and tax

Cash cannot fall in a crash, which is why it feels like the safe place to wait. Using Statistics Canada’s monthly 3-month treasury bill yields and the Consumer Price Index from January 1956 to September 2026, see how often short-term cash kept its purchasing power, how much tax decided the answer, and why the account holding the cash matters more than the cash itself.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 7 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

From 1956-01 to 2026-09, $10,000 rolled over in 3-month treasury bills grew to $359,835 inside a TFSA and to $86,076 with interest taxed at 40%. Prices rose 11.97 times, so in January 1956 dollars those balances are worth $30,057 and $7,190 (1.57% and -0.47% a year after inflation); the same cash earning nothing would be worth $835. Across 729 rolling 10-year periods, cash kept at least the purchasing power it started with in 74% of them in a TFSA and 41% at a 40% tax rate. Treasury bill yields are auction averages, not the rate on any savings account, and the past range is not a forecast.

The central idea

From January 1956 to September 2026, CAD 10,000 rolled over in 3-month treasury bills inside a tax-free account bought about three times as much at the end (1.57% a year above inflation). With the interest taxed at 40% as it was earned, it bought about 28% less than at the start, and a little under a 31% tax rate was the break-even. Across rolling ten-year periods, untaxed treasury bills kept up with prices 74% of the time and taxed ones 41%; no ten-year period starting in 2009 or later kept up even untaxed. Cash removes the risk of a market fall, but it does not remove the risk of losing purchasing power slowly.

01

The safe place to wait

When the fear of a 2008-style crash becomes strong enough, the natural move is to hold cash: a savings account, a GIC, a money-market fund or treasury bills. The balance never shows a fall, and interest keeps arriving. The question this guide asks is what that cash did to purchasing power, the thing the money is ultimately for.

It uses the longest consistent Canadian record available: Statistics Canada’s monthly 3-month treasury bill auction yield from January 1956 to September 2026, which stands in for the return on very short-term, government-backed cash, and the all-items Consumer Price Index for the same months. Each month a balance earns one twelfth of that month’s yield. Every result is shown twice: in a tax-free account such as a TFSA, and with the interest taxed as it is earned. The defaults start in January 1956 with CAD 10,000 and a 40% tax rate; you can change all of them.

02

Seventy years in one chart

The first chart divides each balance by the rise in consumer prices, so a flat line means the cash bought the same basket throughout. Prices rose almost twelvefold over the period: CAD 10,000 kept in a drawer would buy what about CAD 835 bought in January 1956.

Rolled over in treasury bills inside a tax-free account, the same CAD 10,000 grew to about CAD 360,000, worth about CAD 30,000 in January 1956 dollars: about three times the purchasing power, or 1.57% a year above inflation. With 40% of each month’s interest paid in tax, it grew to about CAD 86,000, worth about CAD 7,200 in 1956 dollars, a real loss of 0.47% a year. The two lines start together and separate slowly; it took decades for the gap to become obvious. At about a 31% tax rate on the interest, the taxable line ends where it started.

03

Some decades paid, some did not

The second chart puts the compounded treasury bill yield, the same yield after tax, and inflation side by side for each decade. In the 1970s the yield averaged 7.27% a year and inflation 7.54%, so even untaxed cash fell behind, and taxed at 40% it kept only about 4.3% a year. In the 1980s, the reverse: an 11.86% yield against 6.26% inflation left a real gain even after a 40% tax. In the 1990s the yield, 6.41%, was about three times inflation.

Since 2009 the pattern has been mostly negative. The 2010s yield, 0.92% a year, was below 1.74% inflation before any tax. From January 2020 to September 2026 the yield averaged 2.46% and inflation 3.31%. Over the twelve months to September 2026, treasury bills compounded to about 2.3% while the CPI rose 3.1%. What made cash look good or bad was not its safety but the gap between interest rates and inflation in the years it happened to be held.

04

Every ten-year stretch

The third chart starts the clock at every month-end and holds for ten years. The best ten years for untaxed cash began in December 1980, at about 5.95% a year above inflation; the worst began in July 2012, at about −1.47% a year. Taxed at 40%, the worst began in March 1971, at −3.69% a year: over that decade a taxed cash balance lost nearly a third of its purchasing power while never once showing a lower dollar figure.

Of the 729 ten-year periods that fit in the data, untaxed cash kept its purchasing power in 74% and taxed cash in 41%. Starting in 2009 or later, none of the 93 complete ten-year periods kept up, even untaxed. This is the cost that a crash fear tends to hide: losses that arrive one month at a time instead of in a single headline.

05

The account decides more than the cash does

The fourth chart shows how often cash kept up by tax rate and holding period. Over 30-year periods, untaxed treasury bills kept their purchasing power every time; at a 40% tax rate, 43% of the time; at 50%, 16%. The longer cash is held, the more the tax on interest compounds against it.

The Canada Revenue Agency requires interest to be reported on the return for the year it is paid or credited, interest on compound investments to be reported each year as it accrues even before it is paid, and the gain on a treasury bill held to maturity to be reported as interest. Interest is taxed in full at the marginal rate, unlike a capital gain, of which only part is included. Inside a TFSA, CRA says income earned is generally tax-free even when withdrawn. The cash itself carries no tax advantage: the same treasury bill, GIC or savings deposit is fully taxed in one account and untaxed in another. The asset location guide and the taxable interest guide work through that choice.

06

Your rate is usually lower than the treasury bill yield

These figures are an upper bound for most household cash. A treasury bill auction yield is a wholesale rate; savings accounts, money-market funds after their fees and many cashable deposits have paid less, and a chequing balance often paid nothing. Set the gap to 1 percentage point and the full-period untaxed result falls from 1.57% to 0.62% a year above inflation, while the share of ten-year periods that kept up falls from 74% to 57%. Taxed at 40%, it falls to about 24%.

That gap matters most when rates are low. Over the 2010s a one-point shortfall was larger than the entire treasury bill yield in many months; because the model never lets the rate fall below zero, the savings rate then simply earns nothing.

07

Using cash for what it does well

None of this makes cash a bad holding. It is the right place for money with a date and a price attached: an emergency reserve, a down payment, next year’s tuition, the withdrawals a retiree expects over the next couple of years. The history above shows the cost of using it instead as a long-term hiding place while waiting for a crash that may or may not come, especially in a taxable account.

For money with a horizon of many years, the alternatives carry their own risks. A balanced fund can fall sharply, as it did in 2008 and 2022, and its returns are uncertain and come after fees. But its stock part has historically been the main source of long-run returns above inflation, with no guarantee that this continues or arrives by any particular date. Someone who holds cash because a crash feels likely can also stage the move back: regular purchases from each paycheque are simply how earned income gets invested, while spreading an existing lump sum over months is a choice that keeps part of it in cash longer. The crash-warning guide asks how often a warning must be right for the wait in cash to pay, the waiting-for-a-dip guide tests holding new savings back, and the balanced fund guide covers the long-term alternative.

08

What this history can and cannot tell you

  • The 3-month treasury bill auction average is a wholesale yield published once a month; it is not what any household account paid. Use the gap input to approximate your own rate.
  • Interest is credited monthly at one twelfth of the published yield and taxed at one constant rate as it is earned. Real tax depends on brackets, credits, benefits and the year, and rates and brackets changed many times since 1956. TFSAs only exist since 2009; the untaxed line before then shows what a tax-free account would have done, not one anyone held.
  • The all-items CPI measures an average basket. Your own spending can rise faster or slower; the inflation-window guide shows how wide the range of past price increases has been.
  • Rolling periods overlap heavily, so their shares rest on far fewer independent outcomes than the counts suggest.
  • Past yields and inflation do not predict future ones, and nothing here recommends buying, selling or holding any investment.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 27 October 2026. Every chart applies the monthly 3-month treasury bill auction average yield from Statistics Canada table 10-10-0122-01 (vector v122541) and the all-items Consumer Price Index from table 18-10-0004-01 (vector v41690973), January 1956 to September 2026, both retrieved through the Web Data Service on 27 October 2026. The tax rate, the gap between your savings rate and the treasury bill yield, the target and the amount are your assumptions and are held constant; they are not history. Treasury bill yields are wholesale auction averages, not the rate on any savings account, GIC or money-market fund. Nothing here forecasts interest rates or inflation. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope.
